item.title: The new trail leading to Ireland's 'Gate to Hell'
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
The new trail leading to Ireland's mythical 'Gate to Hell' Rathcroghan is one of Europe's oldest unexcavated royal sites. Now, a brand-new walking path is giving travellers access to ancient landmarks – including the cave that inspired Halloween. From the top of Rathcroghan Mound in Ireland's County Roscommon, the view stretches across grassy fields, stone walls and grazing cattle and sheep. While this may appear as unassuming farmland, a closer look reveals dozens of large, circular earthworks and ancient burial mounds. That's because Rathcroghan (meaning "the fort of Cruachan" in Irish) is one of the oldest and largest unexcavated royal sites in Europe. This was the ancient capital of Ireland's Connacht province and 266 archaeological relics are spread across the 6.5sq-km site – including Iron Age ringforts, Ogham stones carved with ancient Irish script and holy wells. But one of Rathcroghan's most mysterious features is a passageway that extends deep into the earth and crosses the mythological veil into the Celtic Otherworld. Known as Ireland's "Gate to Hell", it is considered to be the birthplace of ancient traditions that evolved into Halloween. "It's a fascinating place – not many sites can claim an entrance to the Otherworld," says John Waddell, emeritus professor of archaeology at the University of Galway. Since many of Rathcroghan's monuments are located on private farmland, visitors have historically only been able to access some of its sites by car. But a brand-new 13km (8-mile) Rathcroghan Archaeological Walking Trail now links the complex's main highlights on a looped walking path, giving travellers new access to the land and a different perspective on how these ancient monuments were connected. Rathcroghan's history stretches back 5,500 years. It was an important hub for ceremonial assemblies, as well asfeasts, seasonal celebrations and royal inaugurations. The site has inspired a wealth of folklore. This is where Ireland's national epic, The Táin – Táin Bó Cúailnge ("The Cattle Raid of Cooley") begins and ends. Considered Ireland's version of The Iliad, it recalls a great raid started by Queen Medb of Connacht, an Iron Age warrior who ruled from her nearby palace. "[Rathcroghan is] an ancient royal site, we're not talking about a palace being stuck out on the landscape; we're talking about a site where people came to gather for various reasons – to mark a celebration, the cross-quarter festivals, a marriage, a contract, a death, a funeral, crowning a king," says Rathcroghan tour guide and research assistant Elaine Conroy. It's also sacred ground. The complex is considered one of the three chief burial places in ancient Ireland where the nation's early kings and chiefs were laid to rest, and today it's home to 40 identified burial mounds. Roughly 1km south-west of the main Rathcroghan mound lies Oweynagat cave – believed to have been the home of the Mórrígan, the supernatural goddess associated with the birth of Halloween. The deity appears as a shape-shifter in The Táin and is associated with the festival of Samhain, which marked the coming of winter. This period – which started on 31 October – was a time when the veil between this world and the Otherworld was thinnest, and the Mórrígan and her malevolent creatures ventured from the cave. As a result, people began dressing in disguise so the spirits did not take them. It typically takes three hours to walk the full trail. I started my day at the Rathcroghan Visitor Centre in the village of Tulsk, before then making the 4km drive to the trailhead at Rathcroghan Mound, where the new walking trail starts and ends, and set out towards the "Gate to Hell". Rathcroghan Mound is the site's largest and most accessible landmark, an 88m-wide-by 5.5m-high (289ft-by-18ft) earthwork that has never been excavated. Yet, foundations discovered during geophysical surveys suggest that it may have been used for various ceremonies, such as the inauguration of kings. "This was the centre of Connacht," says Mike McCarthy, an archaeologist and researcher at the Rathcroghan Visitor and Heritage Centre, as we stand at the new trailhead beside Rathcroghan Mound. "We are walking through a landscape of assembly, ceremony and inauguration, and we're in the middle of a very high-status prehistoric graveyard – burial place of the Kings of Connacht. So there is not only archaeology and history, but there's folklore and mythology and literature associated with the site." Waddell, who conducted field research at Rathcroghan, says one of the reasons the landscape is so interesting is that it is saturated with ancient meaning. "The geophysical surveys of [Rathcroghan Mound] have demonstrated that it had a very complicated history, with all sorts of circular structures buried in it and sometimes erected on top of it. It was a great ceremonial site, probably a great circular timber hall," he says. "That's what makes it so special – the myth and legend as well as archaeology, all embraced in the tales to tell." From the mound, I walk with McCarthy towards one of many new stiles whose steps lead over a stone wall to connect the new trail to previously off-limits farmland. After passing an unnamed burial mound, we soon come to Relignaree, a massive 110m (361ft) circular enclosure known as "The Graveyard of Kings". A newly installed sign reveals that this wasn't just a royal cemetery – it may have also been an "elite residence", complete with ringforts and underground passages. Cattle have grazed this land for thousands of years, and continue to do so today. On our walk, we meet a group of cattle with calves, and McCarthy says hikers might meet livestock and curious sheep along the trail. As McCarthy points out, the animals keep the area grazed. "The monuments are here because of farming," he says. "Otherwise nature would have taken them back." Farmers have even installed large scratching brushes for the cows so they don't use the archaeological monuments instead. The 'Gate to Hell' We soon come to a row of trees and scrub, and here, at the base of the trees, is an ordinary-looking ditch leading to the mythical Gate to Hell. Located 7m (23ft) underground and stretching 37m (121ft) long, this limestone shaft was referenced as early as the 9th Century by Celtic monks and has long been regarded as one of the chief portals to the Otherworld – a dimension to which the living could travel. Though the cave is currently closed to visitors for health and safety reasons because of its elevated carbon dioxide levels, I get down on my hands and knees to look inside the entrance to the passage, which is framed by an Ogham stone dating back to the 4th-8th Centuries. From here, the 10.5m-long (34ft) narrow stone passageway leads down to the natural cave. An image on the new information panel at the cave's entrance shows what it looks like underground and explains how this "infamous" cavern was "regarded as one of the chief entrances or portals to the Irish Otherworld" – a mythical place "where pre-Christian societies believed the Sun went at night.” As we continue walking along the trail, we come to the 115m-wide (377ft) circular enclosure of Rathnadarve, where the two bulls meet in mortal combat at the end of The Táin, the Irish national epic. Further on, we cross a narrow country road and see a sign hidden pointing to a grassy mound. It reads "Cruachan Connacht, ancient royal site". This is Rathbeg, where a new information board reveals it was a "Cemetery for Kings". Though it hasn't been excavated, we learn that members of the Iron Age Aos Dána, a high-status warrior caste, could be buried here. I grew up in Ireland hearing about Queen Medb, and even seeing images of her on old Irish banknotes. Walking through this landscape brings those stories to life, and I can almost hear the hooves of The Táin’s two bulls, the wheels of Medb’s chariot or the eerie screams of the Mórrígan. Unlike a mere monument, Rathcroghan allows visitors to immerse themselves in this landscape and understand how our ancestors used it 5,500 years ago. "People are used to the fact that monuments of certain types were places of ceremony and ritual," says Wadell. "Rathcroghan offers the notion that whole landscapes could be places of this sort of ritual memory and activity." – a handpicked selection of features, videos and can't-miss news, delivered to your inbox twice a week.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Where to Eat, Stay, and Play on Easter Island, the Wild, Remote Island in the Pacific
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
At 1,292 miles from its closest inhabited neighbor, Pitcairn Island, and 2,200 miles from continental Chile, Rapa Nui (Easter Island) takes isolation to the extreme. Here, at the lonely eastern edge of Polynesia, the empty horizon seems to curve with the Earth itself. It’s an extraordinary setting for one of archaeology’s enduring mysteries: Why did a group of Polynesians carve nearly 1,000 monolithic human figures (known as moai), haul them across the island to distant ceremonial platforms over the course of centuries, and then topple them all to the ground? There are plenty of theories, and fewer answers. It adds an element of mystery to an already dramatic landscape, and one that has proven to be timelessly alluring. Today, this Chilean territory is essentially an open-air archaeological museum, with many of its enigmatic moai (representations of Polynesian ancestors) returned to their upright positions following seven decades of restoration. Of course to see Rapa Nui only through its superhuman past is to miss much of the story: The island’s distinct Polynesian culture remains a vital presence, particularly in its sole town, Hanga Roa, where nights come alive with cheerful ukulele music and hip-swirling dances. There’s also a vast, vibrant sea, windswept volcanic plains, and a food culture that draws on the island’s rich heritage and maritime setting. As a repeat visitor to the island, this is my guide to Rapa Nui. Unless you sail over on one of the dozen or so annual cruise ships that dock here, including National Geographic Resolution and Silversea’s Silver Cloud, you’ll likely arrive via air at the world’s most remote commercial airport, Mataveri International. LATAM is the only carrier serving Rapa Nui with at least one daily flight from Santiago, 5.5 hours (and two time zones) away. Once on island, visitors typically sleep in the town of Hanga Roa and organize day trips to the archeological sites, which are never more than a half-hour drive from each other. The Chilean Government officially transferred administration of Rapa Nui National Park in 2017 to the Ma'u Henua Indigenous Community, an organization run by elected members of the Rapa Nui community. Recently, they’ve increased entrance fees (currently CH$95,000, or about $100 USD) to stave off overtourism, while establishing initiatives encouraging longer stays, deeper cultural connections, and stronger protections for the fragile moai. Chief among the changes is a requirement to visit all archeological sites beyond Hanga Roa with a certified guide. Consequently, it’s become less common these days for visitors to rent a car (or bike) and explore on their own. Seafood is a highlight of the Rapa Nui dining scene where the tuna is so fresh, you’ll invariably want to eat it raw in a ceviche, carpaccio, or tiradito (thinly sliced in a spicy citrus sauce). Te Moai Sunset makes a particularly painterly version of the latter. Paired with a pisco sour and views over the modern Moai de la Paz (“Peace Moai”), it’s the most idyllic place to wind down during—you guessed it—sunset. Similarly, the mahi-mahi is sublime over roasted Rapa Nui sweet potatoes at the tiki-style Te Moana, while the dockside ceviche lunches at La Kaleta let you watch the fisherfolk in action. Kotaro has long been Hanga Roa’s hidden treasure: a small, quirky Japanese restaurant with an impeccable tasting menu and strict dining rules outlined on the website (no kids or chitchatting with the chef, for example). Neptuno Sunset is another off-piste favorite thanks to its seafront location near the end of the airstrip, slightly removed from the action. Bountiful seafood pastas are the specialty, but do save some space here or elsewhere for a dessert of po’e, a sweet, dense sponge cake made from mashed ripe bananas. Many assume that Rapa Nui will have the jungle-clad hills of other Polynesian destinations like Hawaii or Tahiti. Instead, it’s covered mostly in grassy plains and looks more like Ireland. While there are two fine beaches on the northern coast at Ovahe and Anakena (which is apt for swimming), this is not your standard resort island, and sunbathing is secondary to the mystique of the moai. Rapa Nui National Park has two chief archeological sites from the moai-building era: Rano Raraku and Ahu Tongariki. The latter is the island’s largest ahu (moai platform) with 15 statues often viewed in silhouette at sunrise. The former is a volcanic crater and quarry site where the ancient Rapa Nui designed some 95% of the island’s sculptures; about 400 remain in situ in various states of construction. There are dozens more ahu sites (many with restored maoi) spread throughout the island. The other major historical attraction is Orongo, a stone village perched on the rim of the Rano Kau volcano, which served as the ceremonial center for religious festivals dedicated to the creator god Makemake. Just offshore from Orongo are Los Motu, small islets that were central to the annual Tangata Manu “Birdman” competition from the 17th to 19th centuries, which involved a death-defying race down Rano Kau, into the Pacific, and up sea cliffs to secure the unbroken egg of a sooty tern. Today, Los Motu is a popular snorkeling site where you can ply the gin-clear waters in search of vibrant corals and 142 marine species found nowhere else on earth, including the rare Easter Island butterflyfish. Mike Rapu Diving Center is one of Rapa Nui’s longest-running and most respected operators for snorkeling and scuba diving. Back on land, there are excellent hikes to be had up Terevaka, the highest point on the island at 1,675 feet, or around the barren Poike Peninsula, which holds several little-explored archeological sites, including petroglyphs and an enormous rock carved in the shape of a human face. Modern Polynesian culture is alive and well on this island of 7,750 people. Though there are many souvenir shops with kitschy moai and colorful shell necklaces, for top local craftsmanship, seek out the paintings, woodcarvings, and jewelry at Mana Gallery, on the north end of Hanga Roa. The music school Toki Rapa Nui, co-founded by classical pianist Mahani Teave, offers occasional concerts and guided visits of its sustainable Earthship building, which is shaped like an eight-petal flower. More popular are the evening Polynesian dance shows from groups like Kari Kari and Te Ra’ai, the latter of which comes with a traditional (if highly theatrical) umu feast cooked in an underground earth oven with hot stones. For something less overtly touristy, check out the contemporary Polynesian music at Iti Lafken. For an all-inclusive stay with daily adventures led by local guides, book at Explora Rapa Nui, an architecturally striking hotel about 15 minutes outside Hanga Roa. Of all the Explora properties, this one has the finest food and shrewdest guides. Right on the edge of town, the Leading Hotels of the World property Nayara Hangaroa gives you a bit more flexibility to book things à la carte. It boasts an oceanfront pool, three unique dining concepts, and oval-shaped rooms styled after homes in the nearby Orongo ceremonial village. More affordable options include the centrally-located (and playfully designed) Hare Nua Hotel Boutique, or the lush garden rooms of Pikera Uri Eco Lodge, from which you can explore the island on horseback. In general, prices are significantly higher here than in mainland Chile due to the remote location and lack of local resources.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Chicken Pozole Verde
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This chicken pozole verde recipe puts a whole bird to work, making a fragrant broth and plenty of tender shredded meat in one go. Roasted tomatillos and a mix of green chiles give the Mexican stew its tang and heat; a final swirl of cilantro purée adds fresh flavor and turns the whole pot brilliantly green. The tomatillos and peppers roast while the chicken simmers. Toasting the canned hominy—a tip from Test Kitchen alum Rick Martinez—gives it a flavor “almost like a corn nut.” But if that’s one step too many, skip it—the stew will still be awesome. Set out red onion, cilantro, dried oregano, and lime wedges, and let everyone load up their own bowl. Add avocado for creaminess, or shredded cabbage, sliced radishes, and crushed tortilla chips for crunch. What kind of hominy should I use? Canned white or golden hominy works here. These plump, chewy corn kernels give the stew its hearty texture. Dried hominy needs to be cooked separately before adding it to the pot. What is Mexican oregano? Mexican oregano is a different herb from Mediterranean oregano, with floral, citrusy notes and a hint of anise. We prefer it in this pozole, but regular dried oregano works too. Do I need chicken stock? No. The whole chicken simmers in water with onion, garlic, and spices to make the broth. Before adding the shredded chicken and cilantro purée, taste the broth and season with salt and pepper. Can I make pozole verde ahead or freeze it? Yes. Cook the chicken up to 3 days ahead and refrigerate it in its broth, then finish the recipe when you’re ready to serve. You can also freeze the finished pozole. Take Rick’s advice and stash a quart for your next weeknight dinner emergency. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Heat ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium. Cook 1 large yellow onion, finely chopped, and 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, seasoning with kosher salt and stirring occasionally, until very tender, 12–15 minutes. Add 2 tsp. ground coriander, 1 tsp. ground cumin, and ½ tsp. dried oregano, preferably Mexican, and cook, stirring constantly, until very fragrant, about 1 minute. Step 2Place one 3½–4-lb. whole chicken in pot and pour in 12 cups water. Bring to a simmer and cook chicken, uncovered and reducing heat as needed to maintain a very gentle simmer (and turning once or twice if it isn’t completely submerged), until cooked through and legs wiggle easily in their joints, 40–50 minutes. Step 3Meanwhile, preheat oven to 425°. Spread out 4 poblano chiles, 2 Cubanelle peppers or 2 more poblano chiles, 3 serrano chiles, and 1½ lb. tomatillos, husks removed, rinsed, on a large rimmed baking sheet. Roast, tossing once or twice, until chiles and peppers are browned and collapsing and tomatillos are tender, 30–40 minutes. Let cool. Step 4Transfer chicken to a cutting board; set broth in pot aside. Let chicken sit until cool enough to handle. Pull meat from bones and shred into bite-size pieces; discard chicken skin and bones. Step 5Split open chiles and peppers; remove stems and seeds and discard. Remove any skin that can be easily peeled off and discard. Transfer chiles and peppers to a blender and add tomatillos; reserve baking sheet. Blend until smooth. Stir chile purée into reserved broth and bring to a simmer. Reserve blender. Step 6Spread out two 15-oz. cans golden or white hominy, rinsed, in an even layer on reserved baking sheet and roast, tossing halfway through, until very fragrant and hominy around edges of baking sheet are just beginning to brown, 12–18 minutes. Scrape into pot with broth. Step 7Season broth with salt and freshly ground black pepper and simmer, uncovered, until flavors come together and broth is rich tasting, about 20 minutes. Ladle ½ cup broth into reserved blender. Add 2 cups cilantro leaves with tender stems and purée until smooth and very bright green, at least 1 minute. Add chicken to broth and cook until heated through, then stir in cilantro purée. Taste posole and season with more salt if needed. Step 8Divide posole among bowls. Top with ½ small red onion, thinly sliced, and more cilantro leaves and dried oregano. Serve with lime wedges for squeezing over. Do Ahead: Chicken can be cooked 3 days ahead. Let cool in broth; cover and chill. Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in 2017 as ‘Posole Verde With Chicken’; it has been updated for style. item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to earn and use an IHG annual lounge membership
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The IHG Milestone Rewards program offers useful benefits, including IHG One Rewards points or food-and-beverage rewards at most tiers, and confirmable suite upgrades at some tiers. Plus, you can choose an IHG annual lounge membership at the 40- and 70-night tiers. Most IHG hotels and resorts don't offer club lounges, but if you want to access the club lounge at IHG properties that do have one, you'll need to do one of the following: - Book a room that includes lounge access, or purchase lounge access during your stay - Stay at an InterContinental property while having Royal Ambassador status Also, keep in mind that even if an IHG property upgrades you to a club-level room, you won't automatically get access to the lounge. At IHG club lounges, you typically get complimentary breakfast and nonalcoholic drinks throughout the day. You will sometimes even get afternoon tea, evening drinks and hors d'oeuvres. Here's everything you need to know about IHG's annual lounge membership, including how to earn and use it. What is IHG's annual lounge membership? IHG's annual lounge membership — which you can earn through IHG's Milestone Rewards program — provides lounge access for one member and a guest if you stay at an IHG property with a club lounge. An annual lounge membership gets you access to the club lounge and its amenities during your stay. However, IHG's terms and conditions allow for lounge access to be restricted "due to renovations, closures, or other facility limitations." This membership also doesn't include Club Regent or Club InterContinental amenities or services beyond the physical lounge. According to IHG's terms and conditions, an annual lounge membership provides access to club lounges on qualified stays, including reward nights and free nights. During stays at participating Iberostar Beachfront Resorts, an annual lounge membership gives you access to the Star Prestige facilities and services (but not to Star Prestige rooms). However, an annual lounge membership doesn't include access to the lounges at InterContinental Alliance Resorts in Macao. Unfortunately, there's no quick way to determine which IHG hotels in a particular city have club lounges. Instead, I've found it most efficient to simply check whether a specific hotel displays rooms with lounge access in the room's name or description. How to earn an IHG annual lounge membership The only way to earn an IHG annual lounge membership is to select it as a 40- or 70-night Milestone Reward. You'll earn IHG Milestone Rewards as you reach the following tiers each calendar year: - 20 nights: 5,000 bonus points, two $20 food-and-beverage rewards or one confirmable suite upgrade - 30 nights: 5,000 bonus points or two $20 food-and-beverage rewards - 40 nights (choose two): 10,000 bonus points, five $20 food-and-beverage rewards, one confirmable suite upgrade (limit one) or one annual lounge membership (limit one) - 50 nights: 10,000 bonus points or five $20 food-and-beverage rewards - 60 nights: 10,000 bonus points or five $20 food-and-beverage rewards - 70 nights (choose two): 10,000 bonus points, five $20 food-and-beverage rewards, two confirmable suite upgrades (limit one) or one annual lounge membership (limit one) - 80 nights: 10,000 bonus points or five $20 food-and-beverage rewards - 90 nights:10,000 bonus points or five $20 food-and-beverage rewards - 100 nights: 10,000 bonus points or five $20 food-and-beverage rewards Once you reach a milestone, you'll have 90 days to select your Milestone Reward. If you don't make a selection within that period, you'll forfeit the reward. Once you select an annual lounge membership as a Milestone Reward, it will be valid through the end of the calendar year following the year in which you earned the Milestone Reward. So, if you reached the 40- or 70-night milestone during this year and selected an annual lounge membership, the pass will be valid through Dec. 31 of next year. How to use an IHG annual lounge membership Between earning an IHG annual lounge membership and its expiration, there's no limit to the number of times you can use your membership. When you check into an IHG hotel or resort with a club lounge, show the front desk staff your annual lounge membership. You can find your memberships in your IHG account's "Rewards Wallet" under "Rewards to enhance your stay." Click "Redeem," and show the resulting page to the front desk staff. The staff will then add club lounge access to your room key or tell you how to access the lounge. You can only use your annual lounge membership if you are the primary member of a qualifying stay. An IHG spokesperson told TPG that the member with the annual lounge membership must be the primary member on the reservation so "the hotel will be able to confirm the existence of the Annual Lounge Pass in the account." In addition to brands like InterContinental, where you might expect to find a club lounge, you'll occasionally find that other IHG brands (like Crowne Plaza and Holiday Inn) offer lounges. Is it worth earning an IHG lounge membership? So, should you select an annual lounge membership at the 40- or 70-night milestone? And should you strive to stay 40 nights at IHG hotels to earn an annual lounge membership as one of your Milestone Rewards choices? Unfortunately, the answer isn't always a clear "yes" or "no." My husband has maintained an annual lounge membership since early 2023, so I've visited several IHG lounges during the last three years. All the club lounges I've visited offered a good selection of food and drinks, including complimentary alcoholic drinks in the evenings. So, I've been satisfied with our decision to select an annual lounge membership at the 40-night Milestone Rewards tier each year. However, you'll also want to consider how much you think you'll use an IHG annual lounge membership. Specifically, you may want to consider how important club lounge availability is to you in the destinations you'll visit. For example, we chose the InterContinental Cartagena de Indias in Colombia and the Holiday Inn Singapore Atrium primarily because their award rates were reasonable and we knew the properties had club lounges. Once you decide the value you think an annual lounge membership would provide, consider the value you'd get from the other Milestone Rewards choices at the 40- or 70-night tier. For example, at the 40-night milestone tier, would you value having 10,000 bonus points, five $20 food-and-beverage rewards or one confirmable suite upgrade more than an annual lounge membership? TPG's October 2026 valuations peg the 10,000 bonus points at about $60, while five $20 food-and-beverage rewards will be worth around $100. I've been happy with IHG's annual lounge membership. If you stay at several IHG hotels with club lounges each year, I expect you'll also find it worth selecting an annual lounge membership through IHG's Milestone Rewards program after staying 40 or 70 nights each calendar year. However, if you rarely stay at IHG hotels and resorts with club lounges, frequently travel with more than one other person or don't value lounge access, you might not get enough value from an annual lounge membership to justify selecting it over other Milestone Rewards at the 40- or 70-night tiers.

item.title: Germany's Condor Airlines to bring its striped planes to bigger US cities
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Condor, the German leisure airline known for its striped planes, is changing where it flies. Once known for summer flights to a host of secondary U.S. destinations — like Anchorage, Baltimore and San Antonio — the Frankfurt-based airline is shifting its strategy to serve larger cities and forge new partnerships following the end of a tie-up with Lufthansa. “If you have such a huge long-haul fleet at Condor and you have the geographic situation in Germany, obviously you can’t operate long-haul fleets without feed,” Peter Gerber, Condor’s CEO, said at the Routes World conference in Frankfurt on Oct. 21. Flying Condor Airlines' business class: Are Prime seats worth it? In this context, "feed" refers to passengers connecting from shorter flights onto longer routes. With a large long-haul fleet based in Frankfurt, Condor needs travelers from across Germany and beyond to fill its planes. The airline has been expanding its own network of connecting flights through Frankfurt while also partnering with other carriers to bring additional passengers into its hub. Condor’s biggest new partner is American Airlines. The carriers unveiled an interline agreement in September, allowing travelers to book flights with both airlines on a single ticket and have their checked bags transferred between flights. Reciprocal frequent flyer benefits are not currently part of the equation, but the arrangement allows either carrier to pass off connecting passengers to the other. Travelers can connect between American and Condor at Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and, beginning in May, O’Hare International Airport (ORD). Condor’s sole U.S. addition next year will be new daily flights to ORD from Frankfurt Airport (FRA) from May 14, 2027, through Sept. 12, 2027. The airline will fly an Airbus A330-900 with 30 business class, 64 premium economy and 216 economy seats on the route. Condor’s transformation into a hub-and-spoke leisure airline when Lufthansa moved to end a long-standing agreement that would have sent connecting passengers to Condor via Frankfurt, home to Lufthansa's largest hub. A legal battle over the agreement ensued and continued until 2025, when a court ruled in Lufthansa’s favor. Now, Condor is working to link FRA with what Gerber described as “the most important O and D destinations" — markets where there's strong demand for travel to or from Frankfurt. The airline has added flights to Josep Tarradellas Barcelona-El Prat Airport (BCN), London Gatwick Airport (LGW) and Venice Marco Polo Airport (VCE) from FRA this year, schedules from aviation analytics firm Cirium show. Gerber added a caveat, however, about competing with Lufthansa at its biggest base: "We will never be able to build up the broadness of the Lufthansa network." When asked about future long-haul expansion, Gerber said he sees a significant opportunity in Latin America, especially to Mexico. Condor’s history of operating nonstop flights between Europe and mid-size U.S. cities like San Antonio may be coming to a close. Speaking on the sidelines of the conference, Gerber said that without the connecting passengers from Lufthansa, Condor must focus on larger U.S. markets. That does not mean Condor will end flights to all of its secondary cities, though. Flights to Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC) in Alaska and Portland International Airport (PDX) in Oregon will continue, according to Cirium schedules. Both airports are major hubs for Alaska Airlines, a longtime Condor partner. Members Alaska Airlines’ Atmos Rewards loyalty program can earn and redeem points on Condor flights, giving travelers another incentive to fly the German carrier. Members of JetBlue’s TrueBlue loyalty program can also earn and redeem points on Condor flights. And, in addition to the American tie-up, Condor has a similar interline agreement with Southwest Airlines. All these arrangements allow Condor to reach more travelers without having to operate flights to every destination itself. Related reading:

item.title: INSTRUCTION: Best time to apply for United Chase cards based on offer history
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Chase has an impressive roster of six United Airlines cards, each with its own set of perks and benefits to justify a place in your wallet. Like most travel rewards cards, each United card offers its own welcome bonus to freshly approved cardholders. These welcome bonuses are the best way to earn a large number of United miles at once. That's why it's very important to make sure you apply at the right time. In this guide, we'll walk you through each United card's offer history and when to apply. (Keep in mind that offers can change at any time, and some of the offers on this page may no longer be available.) Note that we'll only discuss publicly available welcome offers here. However, you might receive targeted offers with more bonus miles. The information for the United Club Business Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. For anyone looking to dip their toes into airline cards, the no-annual-fee United Gateway may be a good option. item.title: Copenhagen is opening a stunning new bathhouse along its harbour this December – and it's shockingly affordable
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Copenhagen is a swimmer’s city. "The cure for anything is salt water: sweat, tears, or the sea," Danish author Karen Blixen, who lived up the coast from Copenhagen, famously wrote in 1934. Copenhageners have taken her words to heart since. In the early 2000s, floating swimming pools were introduced to the Danish capital's harbour after the city's shipbuilding industry collapsed. These pools turned an unused space into a playground for swimmers, divers, water polo enthusiasts and boaters, especially on long summer days. In recent years, winter swimming has also risen in popularity as a way to help with mental and physical health. Winter swimming clubs with sauna access along the harbour are typically oversubscribed with lengthy waiting lists. Now, the next time you visit Copenhagen, there's even more reason to pack a swimsuit. The city’s historic waterfront welcomes a long-awaited new addition on Saturday 5 December: a public swimming pool set to become a new landmark along the city's harbour. Designed by Japanese architecture practice Kengo Kuma Associates, Kai is the new 5,800 square-metre bathing house that has been eight years in the making. It promises ten pools in total, including an open-air rooftop pool and a heated onsen overlooking Copenhagen Harbour. Delayed due to the pandemic and its knock-on effects, the pool was originally slated to open in 2021 and now joins the list of architecturally distinct buildings lining Copenhagen Harbour, including the modern Opera House and the Royal Danish Playhouse. Pools will be spread across the several levels of the minimalist interior, with a 25metre pool on the ground floor. The building also offers year-round access to the harbour with designated swimming and dipping zones in and around a timber boardwalk. While the harbour itself can get pretty chilly in winter, the outdoor first-floor pools benefit from a sustainable vertical ground-source heat pump system providing year-round heating. This designer swimming experience comes with a surprisingly affordable price tag for visitors. Tickets are expected to be in line with other local city-run swimming pools – known as ‘water culture houses’ – where entry is typically under 100kr. (about £7.50). Capacity overall is capped at 380 swimmers. The 989 million DKK (£110 million) project was funded by the City of Copenhagen and Nordea Fonden. Swimmers all over the city are delighted with the news, including Copenhagen’s Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling. “I’m really excited about the opening of the Water Culture House,” she said. “Copenhagen needs more swimming facilities, so it’s incredibly important that we are now getting new pools for adults, as well as paddling pools for children. I hope it will become the city’s new gathering point for water-loving Copenhageners and visitors alike.” The original idea for a new pool in the heart of the city came directly from Copenhageners. Surveys had pinpointed a desire for a new, central public swimming pool and the location on Paper Island could not be better. Once the site of a beloved food market, the area had stood empty for years, before being redeveloped to play home to restaurants, cafes and hospitality businesses. Directly across the harbour from the central tourist hub of Nyhavn and accessed by pedestrian and cycle bridge, the new pool brings renewed focus to the area, that links the old town with the rapidly gentrifying former military area of Holmen and the former shipbuilding area of Refshaleøen. More of the best bathhouses in Copenhagen If you are keen to explore Copenhagen’s swimming cultures, the harbour is the place to start – but brace yourself for chilly waters. At Sandkaj in Nordhavn in the north of the city, a demarcated swim zone invites bathers directly into the deep harbour for lane swimming. It’s a great place for a chat with a fellow winter swimmer; changing room access is members-only, but there is space to change on the quay. Warm up with a sauna at Saunanor, where you can also try the distinctive Danish saunagus tradition. Those seeking a more spa-like experience should head up the coast to Skodsborg Spa Hotel. The former sanatorium offers a superlative spa experience with 16 different bathing experiences, including saunas, steam rooms and access to a private swimming jetty on the beach. Alternative public swimming spots include Valby’s Water Culture House, a chic grey building a world away from typical leisure centre design with a slide, lane swimming and a hot pool area.

item.title: United exits Mexico's new Tulum airport, adds 2 more routes from San Francisco
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
It has been less than three years since Mexico’s newest airport in Tulum welcomed passengers for the very first time. Now, United Airlines is pulling out. The carrier on Friday confirmed it will end all service to Tulum International Airport (TQO) just after the holidays. The news was first spotted by Ishrion Aviation. - United’s flights from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) will run for the last time Jan. 2. - Nonstop service from Houston’s George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) will end after the Jan. 4 flight. In a statement, United said it makes “regular adjustments” to its flight schedule “based on seasonality, demand and other market factors.” It’s not the first carrier to have second thoughts on Tulum. The brand-new airport first welcomed international guests in March 2024, and airlines quickly added flights from major U.S. hubs. The airport was billed as a more convenient link to Tulum’s resorts versus Cancun International Airport (CUN), which sits more than two hours to the north by car. But within months, carriers started slashing service, citing disappointing demand. - United had previously ended its Tulum service from Chicago and Los Angeles before this week’s decision to exit the market entirely. - JetBlue has also pulled out of Tulum. - Both American Airlines and Delta Air Lines have cut back service. Delta this winter will offer flights to Tulum only from Atlanta. It previously had routes from Detroit and Minneapolis. American still has flights from Dallas and Miami, though it once offered service from Charlotte, too. All told, air service from the U.S. to Tulum will be down more than 50% versus just two years ago, according to data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. While United flyers will lose nonstop service to one beach destination in Mexico, the carrier continues to expand its largest West Coast hub. The carrier on Friday confirmed it’s adding two new transcontinental flights from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) — both to Virginia. Twice-weekly flights to Richmond International Airport (RIC) will begin on March 28. Service will run on Thursdays and Sundays. That same day, the carrier will launch service to Norfolk International Airport (ORF). Flights will operate on Wednesdays and Saturdays. It’s United’s second SFO expansion in as many weeks. Just days ago, the carrier announced a trio of new domestic routes from its Bay Area hub. item.title: INSTRUCTION: Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping. Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer. Need to make a substitution? - Evergreen ChutneyStep 1To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer. - ChaatStep 2Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper. Step 3Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces. Step 4To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water. Step 5Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately. Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: 12 best things to do in Icy Strait Point and Hoonah, Alaska, on a cruise
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Icy Strait Point will be your favorite cruise port in Alaska — or your least favorite. You might love the densely forested setting of Chichagof Island, which has the world's highest bear population per square mile and is surrounded by waters teeming with wildlife — an ideal destination for touring. Within Icy Strait Point, you can fly down a 5,495-foot-long zip line, dine on fresh Alaskan seafood and immerse yourself in southeast Alaska's history and Native culture. However, if you love cruise ports that drop you into the middle of real-world Alaska, Icy Strait is not that. It's a purpose-built cruise port (think: a cruise line's private island meets a ski resort), and everything there has been carefully designed to entice you to spend money. You will need to walk or take a shuttle to the city of Hoonah to see where real Alaskans live. If you're inclined to pooh-pooh this kind of port, I urge you not to give up on Icy Strait Point. I was impressed with how well its creators made authentic Alaskan elements accessible to cruise visitors at the port. I didn't have to go far to try salmon dip and halibut pizza washed down with a locally brewed beer. I toured exhibits about the salmon cannery that once occupied the site. With a longer stay, I could have gone on a whale-watching cruise in waters so populous that I'd get a 100% refund if a whale wasn't spotted during the tour. Plus, the port's owners, Huna Totem Corporation, are deeply rooted in the local community. Many of the staff you'll meet in port are Native Alaskans and live in nearby Hoonah; it's a popular spot for high school students to work summer jobs. Huna Totem only leases retail space to locally owned businesses (one gallery exclusively sells art by local Alaskans), and proceeds from the on-site bookshop help fund school activities in Hoonah. Don't miss the doughnut shop run by the local Salvation Army, which uses the profits to provide food for Alaskans in need. Icy Strait Point packages authentic Alaska into a beautiful, easily accessible port. Whether your ship stops for an entire day or just an evening, here are the top 12 things to do in port. (Note: Excursion and activity prices vary by cruise line and date, and they are subject to change.) Icy Strait Point has two cruise piers: Wilderness Landing (closer to the zip line) and Ocean Landing (closer to the rest of the port's shopping, dining and activity centers). A half-mile walking trail connects them. You might certainly enjoy a leisurely nature stroll through the woods (keep an eye out for deer), but I think it's more fun to ride the gondola between them. Icy Strait Point has two gondolas — you'll want the free Transporter Gondola. The four-minute ride takes you through the rainforest and over the port's adventure course area. Time your ride, if possible, to avoid the long lines of tour groups. Icy Strait's ZipRider is a superlative ride. The port touts it as "the world's largest ZipRider." I'm not sure what that means, but I can tell you that six side-by-side zip lines run 5,495 feet in length and drop 1,330 feet in elevation. You are both harnessed and seated in a swing chair, so you're upright but not dangling. You'll soar 300 feet above the rainforest as you reach speeds of more than 60 mph on your flight down the mountain. It's truly thrilling — not only because of the height and speed but also because you actually have time to enjoy the ride and take in the views on this long course. As a bonus, you get to take a second gondola ride on the Skyglider Gondola, which lasts seven minutes and takes you to the top of Hoonah Mountain. The area near Point Adolphus on Chichagof Island is known for its large summertime population of humpback whales. Boats depart Icy Strait Point on multiple whale-watching excursions each day to reach these wildlife-filled waters. In fact, the area is home to so many whales that Huna Totem says every whale-watching tour has seen whales since Icy Strait Point opened in 2004. They are so certain you will see a whale that they will refund 100% of the tour cost if you don't. More expensive tours combine whale watching with seafood feasts or bear-watching excursions. If land mammals are more your thing, Chichagof Island is also known for its grizzly bear population. You can (safely) see one in the wild by signing up for a bear search. These tours take guests to the Spasski River Valley, where you'll walk along designated paths to viewing platforms in the hopes of spotting the large brown bears. You might also see deer, eagles and other wildlife. The waters around Icy Strait Point are full of halibut, so if you're eager to try your hand at ocean fishing in Alaska, you can sign up for a tour. Each fishing boat can take up to six guests, and while you must man your own pole, you'll need to release any fish you catch. (So, don't think you can take your catch back to the ship for dinner.) A fishing tour here is also a miniature wildlife cruise, so you might spot whales, porpoises, sea lions and other aquatic animals while you're out on the water. For a hands-on tour that gives you a literal taste of Alaska, don't miss Icy Strait Point's "In Alaska's Wildest Kitchen" excursion. Guided by local cooks, you'll learn how to prepare local fish (most likely salmon and halibut) by filleting it and then cooking pieces over an open-air grill. Back inside, you'll get to taste the dishes and take home the recipe cards. Some folks just want to enjoy Alaska's wealth of seafood without having to catch and prepare it. Luckily, there are plenty of ways to fill your bellies with fish in Icy Strait Point. You could sign up for a tour that includes a seafood feast of shrimp and crab, Andouille sausage, veggies and s'mores for dessert, often combined with a tribal show. Or, you could grab a bite to eat at one of the port's three waterfront restaurants, food trucks and other food sellers. Duck Point Smokehouse Restaurant by the Ocean Landing dock has cozy fireplace-side indoor seating and an outdoor patio, plus a bar serving Alaskan brews (including the delicious made-on-island Cannery Red Ale). This is where I enjoyed a smoked salmon dip with Parmesan toast points for dipping and my first-ever halibut pizza. Over by the Cannery, The Cookhouse restaurant is the place to go for halibut fish-and-chips and salmon BLT sliders, while the Crab House specializes in locally harvested Dungeness and Alaska snow crab. The go-to drink is the Alaska Crabby bloody mary, garnished with crab meat, shrimp, pickled Alaska beach asparagus and an actual crab leg. At the base of the SkyPeak Gondola, you can stop by the Wild Tacos food truck for shrimp and halibut tacos, among other non-seafood options. Or, more specifically, learn about the salmon canning process and the history of the salmon industry in Hoonah. The Hoonah Cannery buildings, which now house restaurants and shops, were once the site of a salmon canning operation. Spend some time taking in the free museum displays featuring photographs, machinery and other memorabilia from when these buildings housed a factory. While you're at the cannery, you won't want to miss the chance to purchase souvenirs at shops exclusively owned by Alaskan locals and Native Alaskans. The bigger shops in the main part of the building sell all the signature souvenirs you'll find in any Alaska port, but duck into the discreet shops off the hallway for more original gifts. At Dei L'e.ann, you'll find works by Huna Tlingit artists, as well as soaps, salves and lip balms from Tlingit Botanicals. The Alaska Native Heritage Center, near the cannery, offers Icy Strait Point visitors the opportunity to experience and learn about Tlingit culture. The theater offers performances of the 30-minute "Tribal Connections Show," which you can book individually or as part of a tour (often with the seafood feast). Tlingit folks from Hoonah will perform songs and dances and tell stories to share their traditions with cruise ship guests. Stretch your legs and search for wildlife along Icy Strait Point's various nature trails. From Ocean Landing's Adventure Center, you can strike out on a nature trail (about a 12-minute walk) or walk the half-mile trail to the other pier. From the top of the Skyglider Gondola, you can enjoy the mile-long Hidden Lake Loop Trail (yes, there really is a lake up there). Alternatively, you can meander along the beach path (a good spot for wildlife sightings) or walk the mile-and-a-half route to the city of Hoonah. Speaking of Hoonah, it's the main city on Chichagof Island, and it's home to many of the Tlingit people and Alaska locals who work at Icy Strait Point. If you'd prefer to see a real town and not a developed port, you can visit Hoonah by cruise excursion, shuttle bus or a 30-minute walk. In Hoonah, you can hit up some of the local shops for gifts and souvenirs, try a local beer at Icy Strait Brewing or enjoy comfort food all day at The Fisherman's Daughter. You can also watch local carvers create totem poles or work on canoes at their workshop in town. Price: $10 (shuttle), $85 to $130 (tour with tribal show) You might never have heard of Icy Strait Point before your cruise. However, combined with the neighboring city of Hoonah, it has a wealth of activities and attractions to offer cruise passengers. Having spent just an evening in port, I'd recommend looking for itineraries with a longer stay so you can go out on a wildlife tour and have time afterward to do a little shopping and eating within the port complex. item.title: IDEA: 10 magical Christmas traditions around the world
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Living far away from family is hard at the best of times, but it becomes particularly difficult around the holidays. If there's one thing that makes it a little easier for me, it's being able to mix and match festive traditions from different countries to create something that's uniquely ours. As an Italian living in France with a British husband, I love bringing together the best of each culture for a rather extravagant Christmas. On Christmas Eve, we have oysters and Champagne, as per French tradition, followed by an Italian feast and plenty of Christmas crackers – although I draw the line at Christmas pudding, preferring a simple pandoro over anything else. Whether, like me, you spend Christmas far from your family, are planning to chase the sun this December or are driving home for the holidays, one of the great joys of Christmas is making memories and indulging in nostalgic traditions. All over the globe, different countries and cultures celebrate the season in different ways, marking the holiday with long-established rites and rituals or merging heritage to create beautiful new traditions. Below, we run through some of our favourite Christmas traditions around the world, and ask the Traveller editors about their own personal festive rituals. From seafood feasts on Christmas Day in Australia to surfing Santa’s taking to the waves in SoCal, these are the most wholesome traditions for some festive joy this season. Despite Christmas not being recognised as a national holiday in Japan, the festive season is still celebrated – albeit slightly differently from how you’d expect. As part of a marketing campaign launched in 1974, a few years after KFC first opened in Japan, the brand came up with the slogan ‘Kentucky for Christmas’, and it stuck. On Christmas Day, many Japanese families tuck into a full feast of fried chicken – a tradition so popular that you often have to order weeks in advance to make sure you’ve got your bucket guaranteed for the big day. The original Christmas meal even came with a bottle of wine. Christmas cake is just as surprising in Japan, too – strawberry shortcake, made with layers of sponge, whipped cream and fresh strawberries, is a festive favourite. As you might imagine, food is at the heart of Christmas celebrations in Italy. Every region has its own traditions and dishes, enjoyed on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and throughout the festive season. While northern Italians might tuck into tortellini in broth and other comforting dishes, in the south we go all out. In my family, we have twelve different dishes – mostly fish-based – served for Christmas Eve dinner, before indulging in traditional desserts and an unholy amount of nuts while playing tombola. If there is one tradition that the whole country shares, it's the rather quirky tradition of La Befana – a witch-like old woman who flies through the skies on a broomstick on the night of 5 January, leaving gifts for children to discover on the morning of 6 January, known as Epiphany (Epifania in Italian). Well-behaved children receive sweets and presents, while naughty ones get coal – although these days it's usually sweet, sugary charcoal, which is actually delicious. The real difference between the Scottish festive season and that of much of the rest of the world is Hogmanay. Once Christmas Day is done and dusted, the focus is on New Year’s – or, as the Scots call it, Hogmanay. Street parties in cities such as Edinburgh roll on until the early hours, Robert Burns’ Auld Lang Syne is sung at midnight, and the ‘first-footing’ custom takes place – the first visitor to a home after midnight is believed to bring good luck for the year ahead (along with traditional gifts such as whisky, shortbread or a lump of coal, of course). Traditionally, a tall, dark-haired man is considered the luckiest first-footer. While much of the Northern Hemisphere is wrapping up against the cold, Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer, meaning festive celebrations often revolve around the beach, sunshine and outdoor gatherings. "The traditional Christmas lunch in Australia is usually seafood, a roast ham served cold, lots of salads and then a pavlova for dessert," explains Lauren Burvill, CNT’s senior commerce writer and resident Aussie. "After lunch the classic traditions are to play cricket in the backyard, or if you're lucky, on the beach. It's not unusual to see Santa on the beaches as well, often riding on an inflatable rescue boat from the local surf club. On Boxing Day the country's favourite pastime is to watch the cricket or the Sydney to Hobart yacht race." Forget snowy landscapes and cosy fireplaces – in Southern California, you might spot Santa Claus swapping his sleigh for a surfboard during the festive season. "I grew up in greater Los Angeles, and though December isn't typically beach weather, something uncanny almost always happens on Christmas," explains Megan Spurrell, Conde Nast Traveller US’s associate articles director. "The temperatures spike to the mid-70's Fahrenheit (around 24°C) with shining sun and many families, including my own, end up at the beach. But we also go to look out for a very SoCal figure, known as Surfing Santa. We keep our eyes out at Manhattan and Hermosa Beach, especially near the piers, though I've heard of surfing santas in Malibu and Santa Monica, too. Most are just local dudes with a Santa suit who reliably hit the waves on Christmas morning to entertain their neighbours (and get a surf session in)." While many Western traditions see Santa leaving lumps of coal in stockings for badly behaved children, in Austria it's the terrifying Krampus who comes to punish them. As the folklore goes, the Krampus is a fearsome horned figure with a long, snake-like tongue, who accompanies Saint Nicholas on 5 December, otherwise known as Krampusnacht, the eve of Saint Nicholas Day. While Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with sweets and small gifts, Krampus is said to frighten or punish those who have been naughty. Today, the tradition is celebrated with Krampuslauf parades, during which people dressed in elaborate horned masks and furry costumes take to the streets, particularly in Alpine towns and villages. The folklore even inspired a Christmas comedy horror film in 2015, starring Adam Scott and Toni Collette. In Peru, Christmas Eve, known as Nochebuena, is the main event, with families gathering for a festive dinner and celebrations that often continue well past midnight. "We alternate years of spending Christmas in Southern California with my mom and sisters, and going to Lima, Peru, with my husband's family" says Megan. "Though Peru has plenty of traditions tied to Christmas, perhaps my favourite is the sheer fact (shared in many Catholic and Latin American countries) that the whole affair begins at midnight on the 24th. It can be torture waiting until midnight proper to dig into the feast of turkey and arroz arabe that sits out waiting, but the entire city explodes in fireworks when the clock strikes 12. And then the party doesn't stop until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes at a family member's house or at the city's bars and clubs. It almost feels like a preview of New Year's Eve, just a few days earlier." Dumplings are a major part of Polish cuisine day to day, and Christmas is no exception. The traditional Christmas Eve supper, known as Wigilia, begins when the first star appears in the sky, with families gathering around the Christmas table for a feast that traditionally includes 12 meatless dishes. "My favourite part of seasonal eating has never been the Great British Christmas Roast, but instead 'Polish Christmas', celebrated by my family on Christmas Eve, a haphazard tribute to the Polish side of my family tree," says Olivia Squire, Traveller's features editor. "When I was a child my grandmother used to make pierogi (Polish dumplings filled with mashed potato and cottage cheese) from scratch, which in more recent years has been taken over by my mum and I and usually involves a lot of swearing and tears. It's all worth it when we sit down to eat them alongside a vegetarian version of bigos (hunter's stew – an insult to my meat-loving ancestors), breaded fish and holy wafers, soundtracked by Carol's at King's, my English dad's addition." Forget spending a fortune on Christmas presents – in Germany, the tradition of Schrottwichteln puts a rather amusing twist on exchanging gifts, with friends and family swapping unwanted, bizarre or downright useless objects instead. "For gifts, we follow the German tradition of Schrottwichteln (literally 'junk Secret Santa'), where everyone brings something completely useless, unwanted or gloriously ridiculous, often something they were given once and never knew what to do with. The more pointless, tacky or absurd, the better," Karin Mueller, Traveller's visuals director, tells us. "Our children have grown up with this ritual, and what began as a cosy dinner has become the highlight of the year. They never miss it. Now that they’re young adults, they bring their partners along, and it’s turned into this wonderfully chaotic, joyful, very-London celebration that I’m pretty sure they’ll keep going long after we stop hosting." Across England, Christmas is celebrated with familiar traditions, from exchanging gifts to tucking into mince pies and singing Christmas carols. But each county and neighbourhood has its own customs, too. In some seaside towns, brave locals take part in a Boxing Day dip – sprinting into the freezing sea to shake off the Christmas excesses, often while raising money for charity. There's also the age-old custom of burning a Yule log, traditionally associated with good fortune and protection from misfortune. In Cornwall, some communities gather in local pubs for a traditional Cornish ‘shout’, joining together to sing folk songs and sea shanties. "In the hazy betwixmas period, the days of lounging on the sofa and gorging on Terry’s chocolate orange are punctuated by one magical evening at a local pub for a Cornish 'shout'", explains Lucy Bruton, CNT's social media manager. "A shout refers to the community coming together to sing sea shanties and folk songs in the pub, and the Lerryn (where my family live in Cornwall) shout is a particularly special one to me. The tiny pub feels packed to the eaves with people of all ages belting out some of my favourite Cornish songs – from "Trelawney" to "Lamorna" and, of course, “Cornwall My Home”. It’s dark, cosy and a real slice of the magic of Cornwall."

item.title: INSTRUCTION: From winter sun to supplements: How to actually boost your vitamin D (according to an expert)
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Dreaming of a winter sun break for that vitamin D top-up? As the temperatures start to drop in the UK, you’re definitely not alone. The clocks go back on Sunday 25 October until March, meaning we don’t get as much sunlight as we need for efficient Vitamin D production. "During this time the sun's angle in the UK is too low for UVB rays to reach us in sufficient strength, regardless of how much time you spend outdoors," says Dr Sohère Roked, GP, functional medicine and hormone specialist. Vitamin D is a bit of a topic of conversation right now. The government's National Diet and Nutrition Survey found 18 per cent of adults aged 19 to 64 have low vitamin levels, a figure that rises to 31 per cent between January and March. Sunlight is our main source of it, as UVB rays trigger vitamin D production in the skin. Though food sources like oily fish, eggs and fortified foods contribute a little, they're rarely enough on their own. If this time of year also leaves you feeling flat, it may be more than the grey skies or Seasonal affective disorder (SAD) – a type of depression that follows the seasons, usually hitting hardest in winter – kicking in. That sluggishness you might feel, being prone to colds, low mood and aches and pains could all be a sign you’re vitamin D deficient. “A blood test is the only reliable way to know for certain, especially if you’re feeling run-down without an obvious cause,” she adds. Is a winter-sun holiday the best way to boost vitamin D? At Condé Nast Traveller, we’d never discourage you from seeking a joyful winter sun trap to boost those vitamin D levels. "A week abroad in strong winter sun can genuinely raise your vitamin D levels," says Dr Roked. "However, the boost is temporary, typically lasting only a few weeks before levels begin to decline again once you're back under grey UK skies." Treat it as a helpful top-up alongside your regular supplement, not a replacement for it. And pack your supplements in your carry-on too: "Glass blocks UVB rays almost entirely, even though UVA passes through, so vitamin D production simply doesn't happen behind glass, whether that's a car window, an aeroplane window or a balcony door." Can SPF prevent Vitamin D production? On social media, you'll find people who swear by going SPF-free to let the sun in and boost their vitamin D. It doesn't add up, and it leaves your skin exposed to sun damage. Sunscreen doesn't block vitamin D production as much as you might think: "In real-world use, most people don't apply enough or reapply often enough to block it entirely," says Dr Roked. So keep the SPF on, especially somewhere sunny, where you'll still get that vitamin D boost. Where you go matters, as sun reflection can give your levels a bit of a boost. Snow can reflect up to 80 per cent of UV rays, meaning skiers often get significant additional UVB exposure, sometimes without realising it, which is also why sun protection is so important on the slopes," says Dr Roked. Sand reflects around 15 per cent, giving beach-goers a smaller but still meaningful vitamin D boost too. Altitude adds another factor, as UV intensity increases the higher you go. That makes ski trips particularly effective for vitamin D production, alongside their well-known sunburn risk. Heading somewhere cloudy, polluted or far north, such as a Northern Lights break? Pack your vitamin D supplements. "Pollution and cloud cover both reduce UVB penetration, and higher latitudes mean weaker sun even in summer months," says Dr Roked. “It's a small, easy habit that protects against an unnecessary dip in levels while you're away.” Who needs vitamin D all year round? The NHS advises everyone to consider a daily 10 microgram (400 IU) supplement through autumn and winter. People with darker skin should think beyond winter, though, as "higher melanin levels reduce the skin's ability to produce it from sunlight," says Dr Roked, who recommends a year-round supplement for most people with darker skin tones. Who else might need a higher dose? “Skin becomes less efficient at producing vitamin D as we age, and higher body fat can sequester vitamin D, making it less available in the bloodstream. Covering clothing and spending most of the day indoors both limit UVB exposure significantly. And certain medications, including some anticonvulsants and steroids, can also interfere with vitamin D metabolism,” she explains. This is why testing is key, especially since vitamin D toxicity is more common than you might think. "This usually happens from over-supplementation rather than from sunlight or diet,” Dr Rokhed says. For most people, taking a standard daily supplement is fine, but it’s worth checking where else you could be getting it from; protein shakes, multivitamins and other supplements might be accidentally upping your dosage without you realising. What's the best way to take Vitamin D? Choose vitamin D3 over D2 ideally, "as it's more effective at raising blood levels," says Dr Roked. D3 is the form your skin makes from sunlight, while D2 comes from plants and fungi. Most D3 is derived from sheep's wool, so if you're vegan, look for one made from lichen. "A dose of 1000-2000 IU daily is a sensible baseline for most adults, though this should be personalised based on testing," says Dr Roked. And as vitamin D is fat-soluble, try to take it with a meal containing some fat to help absorption. You'll often find vitamin D3 and K2 sold together, as K2 is thought to help direct the extra calcium D3 absorbs into your bones, rather than letting it build up in blood vessels. Above all, she says, "consistency matters most", which is good news if you're crossing time zones, or just feeling the change in climate kick in.

item.title: IDEA: The 15 Most Haunted Places in the World and How to Visit Them
item.description:

The most haunted places in the world may seem like something out of a fable that defies all logic. No matter where you’re traveling, you’re sure to find some sort of haunted landmark, hotel, even landmark-turned-hotel—and usually a ghost tour to go along with it. Spectral hauntings often come with spectacular history, architecture, and artwork, not to mention proximity to incredible cities and natural beauty.
