item.title: We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee
item.description:
Source: Eater
A version of this post originally appeared in Eater Today, which spotlights the freshest news and stories from across the food world every day. Subscribe now. These days, Bushwick is perhaps best known for its graffiti art, ecuavolley, and queer bars; the Brooklyn neighborhood is famous for its family-owned taquerias, American-Italian pastry shops, and the hallowed grounds of the Girls episode where Shoshanna accidentally does meth and runs around pantsless at a warehouse rave. Situate yourself at the heart of its largest park, Maria Hernandez, and you’ll see a kaleidoscopic blend of ravers, Latino families, and the baklava guy. We’re in the Era of the $200 Cup of Coffee Can coffee join the ranks of wine when it comes to high-end tastings? If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Starting this week, it’s also home to a $200 cup of coffee. Bushwick’s Sey Coffee recently announced that it would be touring a rare Panamanian geisha from Finca Sophia, a coffee farm in Panama’s Chiriquí highlands. Sey scooped up the geisha at auction for $44,275, which comes to $6,325 per kilogram, or roughly $200 per cup. The geisha is billed as extraordinarily aromatic, floral, and juicy; Doug Cohen, Sey’s director of brand strategy, advises enjoying it with a clean palate, completely black, and taking your time with it. “As the coffee cools, different aspects of its character become apparent, and that evolution is part of the experience,” he says. Even among fourth-wave coffee shops where prices continue to climb higher, Sey’s $200 cup is an outlier. “Coffee as a premium product is relatively new,” says Cohen. “For so long, coffee has been treated as a commodity, and its value has been constrained by that perception.” He says that both before and right after COVID, folks were becoming more curious about coffee, and educating themselves on platforms like Youtube, Discord, and online forums about how to appreciate it and “understand just how high the ceiling of quality can be.” The arrival of the $200 cup of coffee from a cafe in a neighborhood at the epicenter of conversations about both culinary innovation and gentrification feels ripe for closer examination. So, how did this coffee end up at this price? “We have been purchasing coffee from Finca Sophia for several years,” Cohen says. “This release really grew out of that existing relationship.” When Finca’s general manager told Cohen that the farm’s yields were down by approximately 95 percent, Cohen says a bigger question was raised: “What does it mean to be a good partner when the people you have built relationships with are facing a difficult year?” Buying up the geisha beans felt like a way to both support Sey’s producer, and further develop what Cohen calls “elevated coffee experiences.” In the 2010s, the artisanal coffeehouse wave washed over the country, and especially Brooklyn, with hipster gusto. Sey Coffee was an integral part of that boom. Initially called Lofted Coffee, it operated out of its founders’ Bushwick loft until it rebranded to Sey in 2017, and expanded operations to its present Bushwick location on Grattan Street. That space has become something of a local icon since; Sprudge called its aesthetic “shoebox crossed with an airplane hangar”; the minimal-industrial, cream-hued interiors hit a very Axel Vervoordt-with-a-cyber-sigil-tattoo note (positive). The shop’s cachet has drawn coffee lovers, artists, yuppies, and artist-yuppies; customers have snacked on the gluten-free pastries from L’imprimerie (and now, post-L’imprimerie closure, pastries from Smør), and often post up with their dogs thanks to the semi-indoor-outdoor layout. Sey is hoping to elevate the coffee shop model to something more premium, with a stated focus on ethics and sustainability. Thus far, it’s earned acclaim for those efforts. Food & Wine named it the best coffee shop in New York and received positive media attention for opting out of tipping, choosing instead to pay its staff up to more than 80 percent above the NYC hourly minimum wage; full-time baristas can make up to $31 per hour in addition to receiving benefits and a share of the cafe’s revenue. Increasingly, coffee is getting the same treatment as high-end dining and tasting experiences. There’s the omakase-style menu at NYC’s Driftaway Coffee, or San Francisco’s Komakase coffee tasting room, both of which steer coffee away from quick consumption and toward a world of degustation that appears to have more in common with pricier wine and spirit tastings. The expansion of “espresso house” chain Watch House stateside is also an indicator: The London-based specialty roaster expanded to a fourth location in New York City this summer, raising eyebrows for its $32 cup of coffee while also reportedly scouting for more locations in Austin, Chicago, and Miami. The emerging demand may be just much about luxury as it is about craft. I can’t help but wonder if the $200 cup of coffee is happening in Bushwick because the Girls-era Bushwickian has grown up and wants more exclusive experiences. Is this what happens when, as culture writer Raven Smith said on his new BBC podcast last week, the indie outgrows its sleaze? “For us, this is not about pushing prices higher for the sake of it,” Cohen says. “It is about challenging how we assign value to coffee in the first place. What is an extraordinary coffee actually worth?” As much as we may lament climbing prices for specialty coffee and espresso, why wouldn’t this happen to the category when so many other aspects of food and beverage — from cocktails to sushi to bread — are following the same trajectory? Higher consumer costs notwithstanding, the marketing of specialty beans does steer U.S. coffee culture away from its productivity-focused consumption and the work-optimized “coffee break.” “Why do we accept that certain wines can command thousands of dollars, yet question whether coffee can have comparable value?” Cohen asks. It’s a fair question, albeit one that I’d answer with another: Once we acknowledge that coffee should command a higher price, who still gets to drink it?

item.title: IDEA: Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island
item.description:
Source: Eater
Recently I spent a few days exploring Prince Edward Island, a place that embraces its local foodways with gusto. There’s a complex history here, with roots in Indigenous Mi’kmaq, Acadian, Irish, Scottish, and other cultures. And if one thing unites these histories, it’s the island’s abundance of seafood and produce, which have helped earn it the nickname Canada’s Food Island. How can you not want to visit Canada’s Food Island? Steal My Food Itinerary: 3 Days on Prince Edward Island Canada’s smallest province is big on fresh produce, pristine seafood, gorgeous views, and warm conviviality. On a stretch of land only about 140 miles long, you can eat oysters pulled out of nearby waters, potatoes grown on local farms, dig into a juicy burger made with PEI beef, and lick ice cream made with milk from the cows you pass along those famous red-dirt roads. That’s a lot of good eating packed into a place you can drive across in an afternoon. I had to structure my visit, therefore, around where to dine, but also include a bucket-list visit to Green Gables Heritage Place. (I am a complete freak for L.M. Montgomery’s novel Anne of Green Gables, set on PEI around the turn of the last century.) I also had to schedule time at the PEI International Shellfish Festival, which promised endless trays of freshly shucked oysters and clams, hot buttered lobster rolls, steaming bowls of mussels, and plenty of entertainment, from shucking competitions and cooking demos to live music and dancing. My husband and I rented a car and stationed ourselves in Charlottetown, the island’s main hub. Prince Edward Island is situated in the Gulf of St. Lawrence, just a hop away from Nova Scotia. You’re never far from the ocean here, and on a sunny day, the air seems to sparkle. The island is known for its red-sand cliffs and beaches, rolling landscapes, fishing harbors, and lighthouses. If you’ve read Anne of Green Gables, you’ll know just how pretty PEI is. We landed late Thursday afternoon, ready to hit the ground running. With just shy of three days, I had carefully mapped out the places I wanted to visit, using Charlottetown as my base. Charlottetown isn’t big, and most things here are walkable within 20 minutes or so. First stop in PEI: Slaymaker & Nichols, a gastropub and inn with the feel of an old-fashioned supper club. It takes its name from the 19th-century circus that once performed on the site. They take cocktail making seriously here. The summery feel of the day prompted me to try the watermelon mule, with hibiscus-infused vodka and chunks of pickled watermelon. I liked it, especially alongside the creamy lobster dip with tomatoes and harissa, and the buttery shrimp pil pil, with lots of tasty little spears of asparagus. I was saving myself for my first lobster roll, which we grabbed up the street in an unremarkable spot. It was pretty mediocre, so I won’t go on about it. But after eating, we stopped into Reddins, a speakeasy that channels PEI’s Prohibition history in a dark, intimate third-floor bar with vintage furniture, good jazz, and whimsical cocktails. Our excellent bartender, AB, told us the space had once been a pharmacy where folks came during Prohibition to get their “medicine” — drugstores could legally dispense alcohol by prescription. We tried a few of the signature cocktails, and the one that stood out was the Pink Canary, with vodka, rose, lychee, citrus, and rosé bubbles, served in a small bathtub. Yup, you heard that right. It was sweet and awfully fun to sip. Tip: You need a secret password to get in when you buzz from downstairs. You can get it online, or just do as we did and ask the hostess next door for help. In the pouring rain, we made our way to nearby Victoria Row for breakfast at local roaster Receiver Coffee. Fuel for the day included strong coffee, a particularly good cup of Earl Grey cream tea, and the Ham Slam, a big fluffy cheddar biscuit layered with a runny fried egg, Black Forest ham, Swiss, and Dijon mayo. We swung by the shellfish festival (more on that later) but the rain wasn’t welcoming, so we got back in the car and drove out to tiny and charming Victoria-by-the-Sea. When I say tiny, I mean it: The town is half a square mile, with a population under 200. Despite the town’s size, Landmark Oyster House, set there in an old general store with pretty green shingles and a steep gabled roof, thrives. Our friendly waiter (everyone is abundantly friendly on PEI) suggested Raspberry Point oysters to start. They hit the spot: medium-sized, briny, and sweet, served with lemon wedges and freshly grated horseradish, which is now how I think every oyster should be eaten. We also tried the scallop dog, with buttery sweet scallops, bacon jam, red pepper aioli, and pickled shallots nestled in a toasted bun. It came alongside a very good, eggy potato salad. After seeing the cheery lighthouse and visiting a couple of little gift shops, we popped into Island Chocolates, a family-run shop and café where bars and truffles are hand-crafted, often using local ingredients like haskap, a berry that tastes somewhere between a blueberry and raspberry. That fruity haskap truffle had a nice thick shell of milk chocolate. Sun out? Check. We spent the afternoon at the festival and got a substantial fix of oysters and clams. The lobster rolls here were stuffed with unadorned lobster meat, then melted butter from a gigantic vat was ladled over the top. For dinner, both our bartender and waiter at Slaymaker recommended North Shore Canteen in French River, a local haunt for sure. (A slew of chefs from the shellfish festival were two tables down from us.) The menu, which changes with the current haul, hit on the day’s best ingredients: halibut, striped bass, the aforementioned shellfish, beef, and potatoes. We opted for a very generous portion of local beef tartare, amazingly tasty with capers, roasted garlic, and freshly grated Parmesan, served with Covered Bridge potato chips. We wanted to try more PEI beef and opted for a juicy hanger steak with chimichurri and black garlic, which showcased it well. Dessert was a must: parsnip cake drizzled with caramel sauce for the win. It was time for me to check Green Gables off my bucket list. This is an article about where to eat, so suffice it to say that if you’re a fan, this is 100 percent worth a visit to see the house, wander the Haunted Wood and Lover’s Lane, and taste some nonalcoholic raspberry cordial (IYKYK). All that walking made me hungry, which was good because this was a much anticipated two-lunch day. First stop: Blue Mussel Café, a bright and very welcoming, beloved PEI restaurant set just back from the water in Rustico Harbor. I think it’s obvious what to order, and for good reason: These are excellent mussels — plump, fresh, and brought to the table piled high in a large stainless steel bowl. You can have them prepared with rosemary and lemon or beer and wine. I’d rate them equally, but I did like the hit of rosemary. Melted butter comes in a small ramekin on the side; I used it to dip each mussel, and my husband poured it all over the top. I didn’t have it, but the other signature, seafood chowder, looked popular. It’s made with haddock, salmon, scallops, mussels, and PEI potatoes, and served with a giant biscuit. Noted for my next visit. We hightailed it to our next meal because I had yet to have the perfect lobster roll. Richard’s Fresh Seafood in Covehead Wharf delivered. This is one of the island’s longest-running fish shacks, where you can savor fish and chips and beer on the deck overlooking the fishing boats, or camp out on the nearby beach under the lighthouse with a lobster roll. no mistake: This is the quintessential lobster roll. It was an exercise in abundance, packed with sweet lobster meat that managed to be chunky and fine, bound with lemon and chive mayo and tiny bits of onion, all stuffed in a buttery toasted bun. It came with crunchy coleslaw, crispy fries, and a paper cup of ketchup. There are other menu items, but this lobster roll alone is worth the trip to PEI. For our final dinner, we drove back toward North Rustico Harbor to Rustico Cannery, which opened this past spring. The airy, modern space has giant windows and a big deck that takes in super sunset views. I needed greens, and Rustico delivered. We had crisp romaine hearts with a creamy, spicy charred jalapeño dressing, lardons, Parmesan, and sourdough crunchies. My husband hit the jackpot with his dinner: panko crusted, pan-fried haddock with pickled beet remoulade, jalapeño relish, confit potatoes, and coleslaw. I’d be remiss if I didn’t include our multiple visits to Cows Creamery, the island’s local ice cream shop, which — conveniently — has locations across PEI. It sources the milk for the ice cream from small, local dairy farms and the results are winning! A few standouts were Coffee Cowrunch (English toffee and Oreo), Cownadian Maple (a triple hit of maple ice cream, maple swirl, and maple cookie chunks; when in Rome), and Messie Bessie, chocolate ice cream with Oreo, toffee, and Cow Chips — the thick, ruffled local potato chips covered with rich milk or dark chocolate that are for sale by the bag all over the island. A final note: Many places are seasonal, so check if they’re open if you’re visiting in cooler months.

item.title: IDEA: A New York City Weekend Guide for Design Lovers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
The thing that makes visiting (or living in) New York worth every penny is that you don’t have to go out of your way looking for inspiration. You might be struck by a vintage sign advertising color TVs in the East Village; a grandpa on the Upper East Side pairing bright red socks with his loafers; or that never-gets-old view of the Brooklyn Bridge from an elevated subway track. Design is, indeed, everywhere in NYC, but sometimes you need a bit of a roadmap to plot your next moment of awe. Like many New Yorkers, I derive a lot of joy from looking at pretty things and existing in cool spaces. When I feel like I’m staring at a blank page—or I just want to spend a weekend more intentionally—the places below are the ones I turn to for a creative spark. These spots span boroughs and cover art, architecture, and fashion—from former artist residences and Japanese-inspired stationery stores to restaurants and spas with covetable interiors. For the aesthetes who have already seen the latest exhibition at MoMA, this weekend guide for design lovers is intended to point you in a few other directions (and no, this does not include that viral room full of dirt in SoHo). For many New Yorkers, to go uptown is to go to the museum. And while the Metropolitan Museum of Art holds down the fort, there are a few other players along Museum Mile that always seem to take me by surprise whenever I visit. The Cooper Hewitt, for instance, showcases “design objects” in the broadest sense that span across centuries—you might find an Egyptian ceramic from 1100 BCE in one room, and a Swedish midcentury-modern lamp in another. It’s also a lovely hangout spot; earlier this year, the museum hosted a Hi-Fi listening room, and when the weather’s nice, visitors can take advantage of the garden (tickets are not required and Wi-Fi is free), admiring the gorgeous architecture of Andrew Carnegie’s former mansion. A short walk away, the Neue Galerie, which specializes in early 20th-century German and Austrian art, is where I go to gush over furniture designed by the likes of Josef Hoffmann and Adolf Loos. The museum is set to reopen on November 12 for its 20th anniversary, but in the meantime, you can visit the stunning Café Sabarsky—the Viennese restaurant located within the museum—and pretend you’re at the helm of the next great intellectual movement with your friends over fancy whipped-cream-topped coffees. Further downtown, in Midtown East, the Paul Rudolph Institute is a must for anyone who enjoyed The Brutalist. Join the monthly open house at the Rudolph-designed duplex within the iconic Modulightor building, once the headquarters of the lighting company the architect co-founded with his life partner, Ernst Wagner. Docents are on-site to answer any questions as you wind your way through the all-white apartment, with its disjointed staircases and built-in shelving units, though private tours are also available. When it comes to shopping, I believe one can gain a lot from staring into the windows along Madison Avenue, or even heading inside to get a feel for the luxe fabrics, sans purchase. But for second-hand designer clothing, Upper East Vintage (by appointment only) and Designer Revival (Gentleman’s Resale is also right next door), both on the Upper East Side, are your best bet. I’m also always delighted by what I find at Spellman Gallery, a small showroom owned by an art appraiser with fantastic taste—you can discover all kinds of treasures, from a rare vinyl record to a painting worth a few thousand. Browsing beautiful items will inevitably stir up an appetite, and for a restaurant that has tables equipped with landlines during live art auction sales, check out Marcel 945 Madison, housed inside the historic Breuer Building that is now the global headquarters of Sotheby’s. While the restaurant serves (very expensive) French bistro fare, it’s all about the rotating art on the walls—including works by Roy Lichtenstein and Willem de Kooning, to name a few past residents—which are also available for purchase. If you prefer to walk amongst grittier cast-iron buildings or people-watch from plastic stools, then it’s best you head downtown. Start with a trip to the Judd Foundation, where you can book a slot to explore 37 of minimalist Donald Judd’s artworks, each permanently installed in the late artist’s former residence and studio on Spring Street, and get a glimpse of how an artist lived and breathed in SoHo before the luxury flagships arrived. Over in Greenwich Village, the Renee and Chaim Gross Foundation boasts over 12,000 of American artist Chaim Gross’s sculptures, drawings, and prints, as well as his personal collection of global art. The late artist’s personal home, which he shared with his wife Renee, is light-filled and lived-in—an intimate experience that cannot be replicated at a traditional museum. The Lower East Side, specifically Orchard Street, is where to go to shop independent designers. Browse Colbo—more of a multidisciplinary space than a retail store—for unisex neutrals as you sip an espresso. Adjacent to the shop, Colbo Next Door is a great spot to grab a glass of wine and listen to vinyl. Further along Orchard Street, you’ll find Lara Koleji for vintage Miu Miu, as well as Tumbao, a curation of the very best in Latin American fashion design. On East Broadway, also in the LES, Aeon Bookstore is one of my favorite bookstores in New York, a basement-level shop with a small-but-mighty selection of used titles, whether you’re looking for a coffee table book on the Bauhaus or a beautiful edition of Lolita. Gem Home on Mott Street saves the day whenever I’m in need of a unique, last-minute gift—say, a stainless steel ice cream bowl or spiral toothbrush holder—and the shop, which is also a café, has recently started hosting dinners in collaboration with French pop-up Mon Petit Canard. Continuing on with the theme of downtown cool, Bridges is a swoon-worthy restaurant space that’s bound to get your interior design wheels turning, and there’s a famous Comté cheese tart that’s a work of art in and of itself. If you’re spending a day in Brooklyn, make sure to pop over to the New York Transit Museum in Downtown Brooklyn—talk about a celebration of design. In addition to touring over 20 different vintage train cars, you’ll view an otherwise quotidian part of New York City life in a new light. Graphic design nerds in particular will geek out over the exhibits dedicated to Massimo Vignelli, who designed the 1972 subway map we love and use today. For a different kind of museum experience, Pioneer Works in Red Hook was born out of a former 1866 red-brick warehouse, and today it’s dedicated to all kinds of arts and science programming. On view right now, for instance, is a multimedia exhibition by Helsinki-based artist Tuomas A. Laitinen, drawing on more than a decade of research on octopus intelligence, sleep, and consciousness. There’s only one place I trust for buying jeans, and it’s Front General Store's Outpost, which boasts an entire wall of vintage Levi’s and then some—think worn-in Burberry trench coats, military deadstock, and new shoes from Japanese or British brands you might not have heard of. The vintage shopping in Brooklyn, of course, doesn’t stop there: 10 ft Single by Stella Dallas in Williamsburg is a reliable favorite for threadbare T-shirts and Ralph Lauren sweaters, and if you’re on the hunt for a conversation starter of a chair, Dream Fishing Tackle in Greenpoint is part fishing supply center, part midcentury-modern furniture store. If it wasn’t already clear, NYC loves a retail space that’s also something else: Chyelle in Bushwick and Apartment Ra’el in Bed-Stuy both serve up coffee and beautiful homeware. For those obsessed with paper and pens (guilty), Yoseka Stationery in Greenpoint stocks the very best in Japanese stationery design—from Hobonichi journals to Kaweco fountain pens. In a sea of white-marbled wellness spaces, Spencer’s Spa in Williamsburg proves good design is integral to relaxation. I’ve had excellent facials at both the Brooklyn and SoHo locations, lingering for as long as possible afterwards in the lounge areas, which seem to take inspiration from traditional Japanese, Art Deco, and Scandinavian design (I like to take pictures of all the unique lamps and objects so I can reverse image search them for my apartment later on). But if you’d rather find your zen within New York City’s nightlife scene, James Murphy–owned club Nightmoves in Williamsburg, music venue Public Records in Gowanus, and listening bar Eavesdrop in Greenpoint all boast incredibly impressive custom sound design. A trip to Queens would not be complete without a visit to the Noguchi Museum in Astoria, where you can feel a sense of serenity walking around Isamu Noguchi’s biomorphic sculptures, then buy one of his Akari light sculptures in what is perhaps the best museum gift shop in New York City. While the museum is home to its own sculpture garden, there’s also one practically across the street—make sure you allot some time to strolling Socrates Sculpture Park, where you’ll encounter a whole host of experimental installations (they’re always rotating), with the Manhattan skyline as the backdrop. In Long Island City, the industrial hub-turned-creative enclave in western Queens, MoMA PS1 is at once nostalgic and of-the-moment, showcasing contemporary art within former elementary school halls—it’s especially fun in the summer when it's running its Warm Up series, when everyone gathers outside for DJ sets and music performances. Also in the neighborhood, Somerset House is a staging and interior design gallery that sells collectible furniture and art—think Pierre Jeanneret armchairs and Poul Henningsen lamps—by appointment only. For something a bit more accessible, Lichen in Ridgewood sells a similar catalog of vintage furniture, plus its own in-house designs ranging from glass coffee tables to futuristic sconces. - Get crafty: Take part in an upholstery workshop with For Example and bring home your own stool. - Head to a festival: See inside buildings usually closed to the public during the annual Open House New York festival. - Catch a vintage show: Check the calendar to see when the traveling Manhattan Vintage Show is back in town next. - Do a day trip: Take the Metro-North to New Canaan and see Philip Johnson’s Glass House, or to Cold Spring to visit Russel Wright’s Manitoga. - Go on an art run: Follow Literary Sport for routes that take you around the city’s public sculptures.

item.title: PROFILE: This Sound Map Will Transport You to the PCT From Anywhere
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine
Most backpackers memorialize their trips through photographs. But when LA-based hiker Tom Kelly hit the PCT in 2023, he wanted to document a different, more sensory experience of the trail. Kelly, a nature sound field recordist, composer, and musician, toted 40 ounces of audio recording equipment during his 2,650-mile thru-hike, pausing along the trail to capture the acoustics of the journey. Kelly set up his microphones along burbling creeks and amid chirping insects; he recorded the rustling of grass in the wind, rain on a tent fly, or the chatter of passing hikers. Upon completing his thru-hike, Kelly spent two years compiling his recordings into an interactive and freely accessible sound map. Reporter Amelia Arvesen spoke to Kelly about his project, the challenges of capturing sound in the backcountry, and what he hopes listeners can gain from the map. Tom Kelly: It was beautifully calm, really nice day. And we all went to bed, and I woke up to the sound of a great horned owl calling across the lake. And so, the last thing I want to do is wake up and do something, you know? It’s hard enough to wake up to go to the bathroom, much less take your recording equipment, go hike, set up, and you know, do the whole recording process. I’m a nature sound field recordist, I’m a composer, and music performer based in Los Angeles, California. What led me to recording sound on the PCT is kind of the natural history I have of recording sound in spaces that I would travel to in general. Leading up to the PCT, I’ve always had a field recorder with me because it is just very natural for me to bring it along as my way to interface with the space that I’m in. Getting to the Pacific Crest Trail, I knew that this was going to be my method of creativity while I was hiking. When I set out, I didn’t necessarily know what the project was going to be, or if there was even going to be a project to begin with. But I knew that I wanted to engage in the practice of listening and recording sound along the trail. In the Mojave Desert, on the north side of the LA Aqueduct, I just sat down on the ground, pulled out my recorder, and started listening. And it was in that moment that I became very aware of where I was and what I was doing. And honestly, I could not be happier in that moment. Comparing the scale of these things—like this massive trail, and then here’s like this little moment—and it’s just, for me, taking in kind of just the depth of those small moments all along the trail is something that’s been really rewarding for me, and has been something I’ve worked through this project to try and convey, and offer as a gift to everyone. I hope that when someone sets out to interact with the sound map that I’ve put out there, that they’re able to get just a little piece of what I was able to experience out there. And that is just the ability to slow down and just really experience nature along the Pacific Crest Trail in this kind of embodied sort of way.
